hero.title: File:No Gun Ri bullet marks.jpg
hero.description: This 2008 photo shows a concrete abutment outside one of the twin underpasses of the No Gun Ri railroad bridge, where investigators' white paint identifies bullet marks and embedded fragments from U.S. Army gunfire in the 1950 massacre of South Korean refugees trapped beneath the bridge. Others are similarly marked inside the tunnel. Still other evidence lies beneath the level of the road, built years after the killings.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri - Excerpt of Ambassador Muccio letter.png
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri - Excerpt of Ambassador Muccio letter.png
gallery.credit: The U.S. National Archives and Records Administration
gallery.source: No Gun Ri - Excerpt of Ambassador Muccio letter
gallery.description: In this excerpt of his 1950 letter to Dean Rusk, John J. Muccio, U.S. ambassador to South Korea, informs the assistant secretary of state the U.S. Army has decided to fire on South Korean refugees approaching U.S. lines despite warning shots. The letter is dated July 26, the day the Army's 7th Cavalry Regiment began shooting refugees at No Gun Ri.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri bridge-1960.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri bridge-1960.jpg
gallery.artist: No Gun Ri International Peace Foundation
gallery.credit: No Gun Ri International Peace Foundation
gallery.description: The twin-underpass railroad bridge at No Gun Ri, South Korea, in 1960. Ten years earlier, the U.S. military killed a large number of South Korean refugees under and around the bridge, early in the Korean War.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri Peace Park-Memorial Tower.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri Peace Park-Memorial Tower.jpg
gallery.artist: No Gun Ri International Peace Foundation
gallery.credit: No Gun Ri International Peace Foundation
gallery.source: No Gun Ri Peace Park-Memorial Tower
gallery.description: The Memorial Tower in the No Gun Ri Peace Park, with its three- and two-dimensional depictions of the refugees of 1950, and two arches representing the No Gun Ri tunnel entrances. The 29-acre park, adjacent to the massacre site in Yongdong County in central South Korea, opened in October 2011. It also contains a museum and a peace education center.

gallery.description: A depiction of the scene under the No Gun Ri bridge from the 2009 South Korean feature film ``A Little Pond.’’ The U.S. military killed a large number of South Korean refugees under and around the bridge in July 1950.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri cemetery.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri cemetery.jpg
gallery.description: This cemetery, opened in 2009, holds remains of some victims of the 1950 refugee massacre at No Gun Ri. It occupies a hilltop above the No Gun Ri Memorial Peace Park.

gallery.filename: 1st Cavalry Division troops withdraw, July 29, 1950.jpg
gallery.title: File:1st Cavalry Division troops withdraw, July 29, 1950.jpg
gallery.description: U.S. 1st Cavalry Division troops withdraw southward on July 29, 1950, the day a division battalion pulled back from No Gun Ri after killing large numbers of trapped South Korean refugees there.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri-8th Cavalry.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri-8th Cavalry.jpg
gallery.description: This is an extraneous file. See File:No Gun Ri 06 - 8th Cavalry 24 July - Fire on refugees.jpg

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 01 - USAF 20 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 01 - USAF 20 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report from July 20, 1950, in item 8, lines 3-7, says U.S. Air Force planes strafed "people in white,"' South Korean civilians, at the direction of a ground controller ("Angelo Yoke"). The mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri began six days later with an air attack. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 02 - USAF 20 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 02 - USAF 20 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report from July 20, 1950, in item 8, lines 5-6, says U.S. Air Force planes strafed people "who could have been refugees" on orders of an airborne controller.  The mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri began six days later with an air attack. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 03 - USAF 31 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 03 - USAF 31 July - Refugees strafed.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report from July 31, 1950, in item 8, last two lines, says U.S. Air Force planes strafed people who "appeared to be evacuees." The mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri just days earlier began with an air attack. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 05- US Navy 25 July - Report strafing civilians.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 05- US Navy 25 July - Report strafing civilians.jpg
gallery.description: The operations report for the U.S. Navy aircraft carrier Valley Forge notes in the July 25, 1950, summary (paragraph 4, lines 7-11) that Navy pilots had instructions from the Army to attack any group of more than eight to 10 people in South Korea. This was one day before the mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri began with an air attack. The Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report did not acknowledge this Army policy of indiscriminate attack.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 04 - USAF 25 July - Memo tells of policy to strafe refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 04 - USAF 25 July - Memo tells of policy to strafe refugees.jpg
gallery.description: A memo from Col. Turner C. Rogers, U.S. Fifth Air Force deputy for operations and intelligence, notes in paragraphs 3-4 that Air Force planes are strafing refugees approaching U.S. positions, complying with an Army request. The memo was written on July 25, 1950, one day before the mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri began with such an air attack. The Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report omitted the crucial paragraph 4 from its description of this memo. There is no evidence Col. Rogers' recommendation was followed.

gallery.filename: New 8thcav.jpg
gallery.title: File:New 8thcav.jpg
gallery.description: This is an extraneous file. See File:No Gun Ri 06 - 8th Cavalry 24 July - Fire on refugees.jpg

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 09 - USAF 26 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 09 - USAF 26 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report says, in item 7b, that 50 to 100 "troops" were killed or wounded by U.S. Air Force planes "three miles south" of Yongsan-ni (item 8; misspelled as Yonsan-ni) on July 26, 1950, when survivors estimate 100 South Korean refugees were killed in an air attack at the start of the mass killing of civilians at No Gun Ri, 4 1/2 miles southeast of Yongsan-ni. The Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report did not disclose the existence of this and similar reports.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 07 - Eighth Army 26 July - Stop all refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 07 - Eighth Army 26 July - Stop all refugees.jpg
gallery.description: At 10 a.m. on July 26, 1950, just hours before the U.S. mass killing of South Korean refugees began at No Gun Ri, Eighth Army headquarters sent this message to front-line units about refugee movements. Line 4 says, "No repeat no refugees will be permitted to cross battle lines at any time."

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 08 - USAF 26 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 08 - USAF 26 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report says, in item 8, that U.S. planes "hit road 3 miles southeast" of Yongam-ni on July 26, 1950, the day the U.S. mass killing of South Korean refugees began at No Gun Ri, where they were the target of at least one air attack. The road closest to that location is the dirt road at No Gun Ri. The Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report did not disclose the existence of this and similar reports.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 10 - USAF 27 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 10 - USAF 27 July - Air strike.jpg
gallery.description: An after-mission report says, in item 8, that U.S. planes were ordered to strafe an "unidentified object" one mile west of Hwanggan on July 27, 1950. The trestle at No Gun Ri, where a large number of South Korean refugees were killed by U.S. air and ground forces July 26-29, 1950, is 1 1/2 miles west-southwest of Hwanggan. Some survivors remember planes attacking them on July 27. The Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report did not disclose the existence of this and similar reports.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 06 - 8th Cavalry 24 July - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 06 - 8th Cavalry 24 July - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.description: The 8th Cavalry Regiment's journal, or communications log, records at 1000 hours, or 10 a.m., on July 24, 1950, instructions from 1st Cavalry Division headquarters to "fire everyone," including refugees, trying to cross the front line. The "G-3 Ln" is the regiment's liaison to the division operations staff. Two days later, the mass killing of South Korean refugees by the sister 7th Cavalry Regiment began at No Gun Ri. The 7th Cavalry's own journal from this period, which would have carried any orders to shoot the No Gun Ri refugees, is missing without explanation from the U.S. National Archives.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 11 - 25th Infantry Division 27 July - Treat civilians as enemy.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 11 - 25th Infantry Division 27 July - Treat civilians as enemy.jpg
gallery.description: Maj. Gen. William B. Kean on July 27, 1950, orders his 25th Infantry Division to view civilians as enemy. The accompanying overlay map outlined an area covering the entire warfront. A day earlier, the mass killing of South Korean refugees began at No Gun Ri at the hands of the neighboring 1st Cavalry Division. In another 25th Infantry Division document uploaded here, Kean's staff indicated his order meant civilians should be shot.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 12 - 25th Infantry Division 26 July - Shoot civilians.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 12 - 25th Infantry Division 26 July - Shoot civilians.jpg
gallery.description: A 25th Infantry Division headquarters journal records at 10 p.m. ("2200") on July 26, 1950, that Maj. Gen. William B. Kean, division commander, has decided civilians in the war zone should be "considered as unfriendly and shot." On this day, the large-scale killing of South Korean refugees began at No Gun Ri, at the hands of the neighboring 1st Cavalry Division. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 13 - 25th Infantry Division 27 July - Drastic action against civilians.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 13 - 25th Infantry Division 27 July - Drastic action against civilians.jpg
gallery.description: In the final four lines of these instructions, the three regiments of the 25th Infantry Division are told by the division's commanding general ("CG"), Maj. Gen. William B. Kean, to consider "as enemy" any civilians in the combat zone and to "take drastic action" to stop their movements. A day earlier, the large-scale klling of South Korean refugees began at No Gun Ri at the hands of the neighboring 1st Cavalry Division. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 15 - 8th Cavalry 9 August - Shoot all refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 15 - 8th Cavalry 9 August - Shoot all refugees.jpg
gallery.description: The log of the 1st Battalion, 8th Cavalry Regiment, records a communication on August 9, 1950, when U.S. troops held the Naktong River line, in which the regimental commander orders, "Shoot all refugees coming across river." The entry is fifth from the bottom, at "1655 hours" (4:55 p.m.). "Scrappy 6" was the code name for the commander, Col. Raymond D. Palmer. This was 11 days after the large-scale killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri by the sister 7th Cavalry Regiment. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 14 - 61st Field Artillery 29 July - Anyone seen is enemy.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 14 - 61st Field Artillery 29 July - Anyone seen is enemy.jpg
gallery.description: A 1st Cavalry Division artillery unit's daily report says, on line 10, "Now anyone seen is considered enemy." It is dated July 29, 1950, the day division troops withdrew from No Gun Ri, after three days of shooting trapped refugees there. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 16 - Maj. Gen. Gay 29 August - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 16 - Maj. Gen. Gay 29 August - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.description: A journal of the 1st Cavalry Division artillery command records an August 29, 1950, communication (entry at "1200" beginning "Fr Capt Frohardt") noting that division commander Maj. Gen. Hobart R. Gay (code name "Saber 6") "orders all refugees to be fired on." This was a month after his division's 7th Cavalry Regiment carried out the mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 17 - Maj. Gen. Gay 29 August - Refugee are fair game.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 17 - Maj. Gen. Gay 29 August - Refugee are fair game.jpg
gallery.description: A 1st Cavalry Division artillery unit's journal notes that division commander Maj. Gen. Hobart R. Gay (code name "Saber 6") called at "1440" hours to say refugees "are fair game."  This was a month after his division's 7th Cavalry Regiment carried out the mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun Ri. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.

gallery.filename: No Gun Ri 18 - 35th Infantry 17 August - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.title: File:No Gun Ri 18 - 35th Infantry 17 August - Fire on refugees.jpg
gallery.description: A page from the August 17, 1950, journal of the 25th Infantry Division's 35th Infantry Regiment says, in Serial No. 16, that approaching refugees will be considered enemy and fired on. This was 19 days after the mass killing of South Korean refugees at No Gun ri by the neighboring 1st Cavalry Division. The existence of this and many similar documents showing a policy and practice of indiscriminate civilian killings was not disclosed in the Pentagon's 2001 No Gun Ri investigative report.
